courses.name: Programming Fundamentals
courses.description: Language-independent basics of programming: variables, control flow, functions, simple data types, and basic problem decomposition.
learning_outcomes: Understand fundamental programming constructs
Write basic modular functions
Decompose algorithmic problems
courses.assumed_knowledge: Basic secondary-school mathematics and logical reasoning.
courses.difficulty_rationale: Introductory level; designed for beginners with no prior coding experience.
courses.typical_audience: First-year computer science, engineering, or general students beginning software development.

courses.name: C Programming
courses.description: Procedural programming in C, including pointers, manual memory management, arrays, structs, and file I/O.
learning_outcomes: Manipulate memory directly with pointers
Manage dynamic memory allocation safely
Implement low-level data records
courses.assumed_knowledge: Basic programming fundamentals (loops, conditionals, functions).
courses.difficulty_rationale: Manual memory management and pointer semantics require careful attention to system behavior.
courses.typical_audience: Computer science undergraduates and systems programmers.

courses.name: Python Programming
courses.description: Programming in Python: syntax, built-in data structures, functions, modules, and file handling, with an introduction to common libraries.
learning_outcomes: Write idiomatic Python scripts
Utilize built-in data collections effectively
Leverage modules and standard libraries
courses.assumed_knowledge: Basic programming fundamentals.
courses.difficulty_rationale: Readable high-level syntax makes Python accessible for beginners while supporting rich idioms.
courses.typical_audience: Students and practitioners entering software development, data science, or automation.

courses.name: Object-Oriented Programming
courses.description: Object-oriented concepts: classes, objects, encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, and abstraction, independent of any one language.
learning_outcomes: Design object-oriented class hierarchies
Apply encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism
Utilize design patterns for modularity
courses.assumed_knowledge: Comfort with at least one programming language and modular decomposition.
courses.difficulty_rationale: Requires shift from procedural to conceptual abstraction and class hierarchies.
courses.typical_audience: Undergraduate students preparing for large-scale software engineering.

courses.name: Java Programming

Utilize the Java Collections Framework

courses.assumed_knowledge: Programming fundamentals and basic object-oriented principles.

courses.name: Data Structures

courses.description: Design, implementation, and use of arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, heaps, hash tables, and graphs, with basic operation costs.

Analyze runtime and space complexity with Big-O

courses.assumed_knowledge: Procedural programming and object-oriented fundamentals.

courses.name: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
courses.description: Algorithm design paradigms (divide and conquer, greedy, dynamic programming, graph algorithms) and analysis of correctness and time/space complexity.

Prove correctness and derive recurrence relations
Classify computational complexity and NP-completeness
courses.assumed_knowledge: Data structures and discrete mathematics.
courses.difficulty_rationale: Requires strong mathematical maturity, formal proofs, and rigorous asymptotic complexity analysis.

courses.name: Computational Biology and Bioinformatics
courses.description: Algorithmic methods in molecular biology: sequence alignment (Needleman-Wunsch, Smith-Waterman), genome assembly, phylogenetic trees, and structural prediction.
learning_outcomes: Implement dynamic programming algorithms for DNA/protein sequence alignment
Analyze genome assembly graph algorithms (De Bruijn graphs)
Use computational tools to query biological databases
main_topics: Genome Assembly via De Bruijn Graphs
courses.assumed_knowledge: Data structures, algorithms, and basic programming.
courses.difficulty_rationale: Bridges sophisticated dynamic programming and graph algorithms with biological domain complexity.
courses.typical_audience: Computer scientists and biologists interested in computational life sciences.

courses.name: NoSQL and Distributed Data Stores
courses.description: Non-relational data modeling and distributed databases: document stores (MongoDB), key-value stores (Redis), wide-column stores (Cassandra), and graph databases (Neo4j).
learning_outcomes: Design denormalized document schemas for rapid querying
Evaluate trade-offs between consistency and partition tolerance in distributed stores
Query graph databases using Cypher
courses.assumed_knowledge: Relational databases and basic computer networks.
courses.difficulty_rationale: Contrasts normalized relational constraints with eventual consistency and schema-on-read trade-offs.
courses.typical_audience: Backend engineers, data architects, and cloud application developers.

courses.name: Blockchain and Distributed Ledgers
courses.description: Architectures of decentralized ledgers: cryptographic hashing, Merkle trees, consensus mechanisms (Proof of Work, Proof of Stake), smart contracts, and decentralized apps.
learning_outcomes: Explain cryptographic immutability using Merkle trees and hash chains
Compare Byzantine fault-tolerant consensus mechanisms
Develop and test secure smart contracts
main_topics: Cryptographic Hash Pointers and Merkle Trees
Ethereum Virtual Machine and Smart Contracts
courses.assumed_knowledge: Computer networks, cryptography basics, and object-oriented programming.
courses.difficulty_rationale: Combines peer-to-peer networking, game-theoretic economic incentives, and irreversible smart contract execution.
courses.typical_audience: Software developers and students interested in decentralized applications.

courses.name: Embedded Systems and IoT
courses.description: Microcontroller hardware-software interface: GPIO, interrupts, hardware timers, communication buses (UART, SPI, I2C), ADC, and low-power IoT network stacks.
learning_outcomes: Write bare-metal C programs for ARM microcontrollers
Interface sensors and actuators via SPI, I2C, and UART
Implement interrupt service routines with predictable latency
courses.assumed_knowledge: C programming and computer organization.
courses.difficulty_rationale: Demands close attention to hardware registers, memory maps, electrical timings, and real-time responsiveness.
courses.typical_audience: Computer engineering, robotics, and hardware-software systems students.

courses.name: Knowledge Graphs and Semantic Web
courses.description: Structured knowledge representation: RDF triples, OWL ontologies, SPARQL graph queries, knowledge graph embeddings, entity resolution, and link prediction.
learning_outcomes: Model domain schemas using OWL and RDFS ontologies
Execute complex graph queries using SPARQL
Train knowledge graph embeddings for link prediction
courses.assumed_knowledge: Discrete mathematics, data structures, and database systems.
courses.difficulty_rationale: Blends formal first-order logic semantics with practical graph databases and modern neural graph embeddings.
courses.typical_audience: AI researchers, data architects, search engine developers, and semantic data engineers.

courses.name: Speech and Audio Processing
courses.description: Digital processing and recognition of acoustic signals: Fourier transforms, Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCCs), acoustic modeling, and end-to-end ASR.
learning_outcomes: Compute audio spectrograms and filterbank features
Implement acoustic feature extraction pipelines
Architect end-to-end deep neural speech recognition models
courses.assumed_knowledge: Calculus, linear algebra, signals basics, and deep learning.
courses.difficulty_rationale: High-dimensional continuous temporal signals require combined signal processing math and deep learning architectures.
courses.typical_audience: Machine learning engineers, computational linguists, and audio technology researchers.

courses.name: Multimodal Deep Learning
courses.description: Architectures integrating multiple sensory modalities: contrastive learning (CLIP), cross-attention fusion, vision-language models, and multimodal generation.
learning_outcomes: Train cross-modal contrastive representations using CLIP
Architect cross-attention fusion layers for vision and text
Evaluate multimodal reasoning on benchmark visual QA datasets
main_topics: Visual Question Answering and Image Captioning
courses.assumed_knowledge: Deep learning, computer vision, and natural language processing.
courses.difficulty_rationale: Requires reconciling disparate tensor modalities (pixels, tokens, audio) in high-dimensional joint spaces.
courses.typical_audience: Advanced AI researchers and engineers building frontier multimodal systems.

courses.name: Linux System Administration and Scripting
courses.description: Practical Unix/Linux administration: file permissions, shell scripting (Bash), process management, systemd services, SSH, package management, and system logs.
learning_outcomes: Write robust automated shell scripts with error handling
Configure user permissions, ownership, and PAM security
Manage systemd daemon services and diagnose system logs
main_topics: SSH Configuration, Firewalls, and Networking Basics
courses.assumed_knowledge: Basic computer literacy and introductory programming.
courses.difficulty_rationale: Command-line driven operating environment requiring memorization and practice with Unix utilities.
courses.typical_audience: All computer science, software engineering, and cybersecurity students.

courses.name: Discrete Optimization and Combinatorial Algorithms
courses.description: Exact and heuristic techniques for NP-hard discrete problems: branch and bound, integer linear programming (ILP), dynamic programming, cutting planes, and local search.
learning_outcomes: Formulate industrial scheduling and routing problems as integer linear programs
Implement branch-and-bound algorithms with effective bounding functions
Apply metaheuristics like simulated annealing and genetic algorithms
main_topics: Linear Programming Duality and Simplex Method
Branch and Bound / Branch and Cut
courses.assumed_knowledge: Algorithms, linear algebra, and mathematical optimization.
courses.difficulty_rationale: NP-hard computational complexity requires subtle mathematical bounding and combinatorial trade-offs.
courses.typical_audience: Operations researchers, algorithms engineers, and logistics specialists.

courses.name: Bayesian Data Analysis and Inference
courses.description: Probabilistic programming and Bayesian modeling: prior/posterior distributions, conjugate priors, Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC, Gibbs, HMC), and Stan/PyMC.
learning_outcomes: Formulate hierarchical Bayesian generative models
Estimate posterior distributions using MCMC and PyMC
Evaluate model fit using posterior predictive checks
main_topics: Bayes' Rule and Probability as Degree of Belief
courses.assumed_knowledge: Probability and statistics, multivariable calculus, and Python.
courses.difficulty_rationale: Requires shifting from frequentist p-values to high-dimensional probabilistic integrals and MCMC diagnostics.
courses.typical_audience: Data scientists, statisticians, and probabilistic machine learning researchers.

courses.name: Deep Reinforcement Learning
courses.description: Combining deep neural networks with reinforcement learning: Deep Q-Networks (DQN), policy gradients (REINFORCE), actor-critic methods (PPO, SAC), and model-based RL.
learning_outcomes: Implement Deep Q-Learning with experience replay and target networks
Derive and program policy gradient methods like PPO
Train autonomous agents in simulated physics environments
courses.assumed_knowledge: Reinforcement learning, deep learning, and multivariable calculus.
courses.difficulty_rationale: High training instability, hyperparameter sensitivity, and non-stationary target distributions.
courses.typical_audience: Robotics researchers, game AI developers, and advanced AI scientists.

courses.name: Edge AI and TinyML
courses.description: Deploying machine learning models to resource-constrained devices: model quantization (INT8), pruning, knowledge distillation, hardware acceleration, and edge runtimes.
learning_outcomes: Quantize floating-point neural networks to INT8 with minimal accuracy loss
Deploy optimized models onto microcontrollers and mobile edge accelerators
Profile latency, memory footprint, and power consumption on hardware
courses.assumed_knowledge: Deep learning, embedded systems, and C/C++ or Python.
courses.difficulty_rationale: Requires aggressive optimization across hardware cache, memory limits, and numerical accuracy.
courses.typical_audience: Embedded engineers, IoT architects, and mobile ML engineers.

courses.name: Information Theory and Coding
courses.description: Mathematical foundations of communication: Shannon entropy, mutual information, source coding theorem, channel capacity theorem, and error-correcting codes.
learning_outcomes: Calculate entropy, relative entropy, and mutual information
Design optimal lossless compression codes (Huffman, Arithmetic)
Calculate the Shannon channel capacity for noisy channels
main_topics: Lossless Data Compression and Huffman Coding
Channel Capacity and Noisy-Channel Coding Theorem
courses.assumed_knowledge: Probability and statistics, discrete mathematics, and linear algebra.
courses.difficulty_rationale: Rigorous probability theory, limits, and abstract asymptotic communication bounds.
courses.typical_audience: Communication engineers, theorists, cryptographers, and machine learning theorists.

courses.name: Algorithmic Game Theory and Mechanism Design
courses.description: Strategic decision making in computational systems: Nash equilibrium, zero-sum games, mechanism design, auctions, Price of Anarchy, and multi-agent coordination.
learning_outcomes: Compute pure and mixed strategy Nash equilibria
Design incentive-compatible mechanisms and auctions
Bound the Price of Anarchy in decentralized network routing
main_topics: Price of Anarchy and Congestion Games
courses.assumed_knowledge: Discrete mathematics, probability, and algorithms.
courses.difficulty_rationale: Combines non-cooperative game theory, microeconomic incentives, and algorithmic complexity.
courses.typical_audience: Computer scientists, quantitative economists, and blockchain protocol architects.

courses.name: Vector Databases and Similarity Search
courses.description: High-dimensional similarity search: dense embeddings, distance metrics (Cosine, Euclidean), approximate nearest neighbors (HNSW, IVF-PQ), and vector store engines.
learning_outcomes: Implement approximate nearest neighbor algorithms like HNSW
Index and query high-dimensional embeddings in vector stores
Evaluate latency and recall trade-offs for semantic search
main_topics: High-Dimensional Vector Spaces and Curse of Dimensionality
courses.assumed_knowledge: Data structures, linear algebra, and basic machine learning.
courses.difficulty_rationale: Balances high-dimensional geometry trade-offs with scalable graph indexing data structures.
courses.typical_audience: AI engineers, search developers, and RAG application builders.

prerequisites.explanation: C assumes familiarity with variables, control flow, and functions before pointers and manual memory management make sense.
Classes and objects build on basic constructs such as variables, functions, and control flow. The prerequisite is language-independent.
Java is class-based, so OOP concepts ease learning it. Java is also taught as a first language, so this is not strictly required.
Familiarity with variables, control flow, functions, and basic programming constructs helps learners understand data structures and implement operations on them.
Algorithm design and analysis use lists, trees, heaps, hash tables, and graphs, and rely on knowing their operation costs.
Induction, recurrences, and counting underpin correctness proofs and complexity analysis. Depth of math required varies by curriculum.
Sets, relations, logic, and proof techniques are used throughout automata and formal-language theory.
Prior programming makes instruction-level concepts easier to relate to code, but many courses start from digital logic without it.
Processes, interrupts, memory management, and I/O are explained in terms of processor and memory organization.
Queues, trees, hash tables, and linked lists are used in scheduling, memory management, and file systems.
OS concepts and labs are commonly presented in C or C-like code; other systems languages can substitute.
Indexing, hashing, and B-trees draw on data-structure knowledge. Introductory SQL-focused courses can be taken without it.
Sockets, processes, and I/O handling help in understanding the transport layer and network software. Many networks courses do not strictly require OS.
Lexical analysis and parsing rely on regular expressions, finite automata, and context-free grammars.
Symbol tables, parse trees, syntax trees, and graphs are core compiler data structures.
Code generation and optimization target machine instruction sets and memory hierarchies.
Object-oriented design is a common basis for software design and modelling, though SE can also be taught with other paradigms.
Continuous random variables and expectation use integration; introductory statistics courses may avoid calculus.
Solving linear systems, matrix factorizations, and eigenvalue methods require linear algebra.
Numerical differentiation, integration, root finding, and error analysis presuppose calculus and Taylor series.
Numerical algorithms are implemented and tested in code, so basic programming is helpful.
Gradients, derivatives, and stationary conditions are fundamental to continuous optimization.
Linear and convex optimization are expressed with vectors and matrices. Depth required varies by course.
Search, planning, and graph-based representations use queues, stacks, trees, and graphs.
Uncertainty and probabilistic reasoning topics use probability. Many AI courses can be started without it.
Propositional and predicate logic support the knowledge-representation topics, but are not needed to begin.
Learning from data, likelihood, bias-variance, and evaluation rely on probability and statistics.
Vectors, matrices, and decompositions support many algorithms. The amount required depends on the depth and type of machine learning course.
Model training is optimization, but applied courses use it as a black box.
Python is the most common language for ML practice, but R, Julia, or other languages can be used; programming ability is the underlying need.
Understanding machine learning concepts, model training, loss functions, and generalization provides useful preparation for studying neural networks. Some deep learning courses are self-contained.
Backpropagation uses the chain rule and partial derivatives; practitioner-focused courses may only need the intuition.
Text classification, sequence labeling, and language modelling use ML methods and evaluation.
Modern neural NLP builds on deep learning, but classical NLP can be studied without it.
Recognition and detection use ML concepts such as classification, features, and evaluation.
Modern vision systems are largely CNN- and transformer-based. Classical-only vision courses do not need it.
Image transformations, camera geometry, and feature methods use matrices and vectors.
Exploratory analysis, inference, and interpreting results require statistics fundamentals.
Python is a common data-science language; R or other tools are valid alternatives.
Association measures, clustering evaluation, and anomaly detection draw on statistics.
Data mining works on stored data and uses SQL-style access and preprocessing.
Markov decision processes, expectations, and stochastic policies require probability.
Function approximation, generalization, and training concepts from ML help in studying RL.
Deep RL combines neural networks with RL, but classical RL does not require deep learning.
Understanding data models, queries, and storage helps in understanding distributed data processing.
Analytics concepts and workflows are scaled up in big data settings.
Virtualization, containers, and resource management extend OS concepts.
Cloud services rely on networking concepts such as addressing, load balancing, and distributed communication.
Many threats and defenses (firewalls, TLS, intrusion detection) operate at the network level.
Access control, process isolation, and memory protection are central to system security.
Cryptography uses number theory and combinatorics, but introductory security can be studied without it.
Generative models such as GANs, diffusion models, and transformers are built on neural networks. Applied courses on using generative tools need less preparation.
LLMs are deep transformer networks; training, attention, and optimization concepts come from deep learning.
Tokenization, language modelling, embeddings, and evaluation are NLP foundations for LLMs.
RAG augments an LLM with retrieved context; understanding prompting, context windows, and limitations is needed.
Indexing and querying concepts help with retrieval components, but vector-search tooling can be learned directly.
MLOps manages the ML lifecycle, so it assumes understanding of training, evaluation, and model behaviour.
Version control, testing, CI/CD, and maintainability practices carry over to ML systems.
Production ML is commonly deployed on cloud infrastructure and containers.
C++ builds directly on core programming concepts like variables, control flow, and functions.
Knowledge of object-oriented principles facilitates understanding C++ class design and inheritance.
Prior programming experience provides helpful intuition for R scripting and data operations.
R is widely utilized for statistical computing and exploratory data analysis in data science.
Functional programming requires foundational fluency with functions, expressions, and evaluation.
Understanding standard data structures aids in appreciating immutable trees and functional lists.
Graph theory relies fundamentally on discrete relations, set theory, and formal proof techniques.
Deep understanding of graph properties enhances the design of optimal graph traversal and network flow algorithms.
Web engineering requires programming fundamentals for client-side logic and backend scripting.
Web frontend concepts provide useful background for responsive UI and API consumption in mobile apps.
Mobile application frameworks heavily utilize object-oriented architectures and component lifecycles.
Distributed systems build on process coordination, concurrency, memory models, and networking.
Understanding socket communication and packet transfer is essential for distributed protocol analysis.
Modern cryptography relies on modular arithmetic, number theory, and computational hardness.
Network protocols provide the operational context for transport-layer security and key exchange.
Cryptographic ciphers form the foundational defense mechanisms for securing digital infrastructure.
Search engines rely on inverted indices, hash maps, and tree structures for efficient query evaluation.
3D graphics rendering is grounded in linear matrix transformations and vector projections.
Low-level shader programming and rendering APIs often utilize C and memory buffers.
Kinematics and coordinate frames require coordinate transformation matrices and vector spaces.
AI planning and heuristic search provide the decision-making logic for autonomous agents.
Parallel programming directly manipulates thread scheduling, mutexes, and virtual address spaces.
C provides direct access to POSIX threads and hardware memory barriers.
System design scales the modularity, requirements, and testing principles taught in software engineering.
Distributed consensus and partition handling are crucial for architecting resilient large-scale systems.
DevOps automates the build, test, and release cycles studied in software engineering.
Cloud infrastructure provides the hosting environment for automated CI/CD deployment pipelines.
Quantum states and quantum gates are mathematically defined as unitary operators on Hilbert spaces.
Understanding distributions and variance is key to choosing honest visual encodings.
Autocorrelation, stationarity, and ARIMA forecasting build directly on stochastic processes.
Understanding model training and loss functions provides technical grounding for assessing algorithmic bias.
Sequence alignment and genomic assembly heavily utilize dynamic programming tables and graph indices.
Understanding relational constraints illuminates the architectural trade-offs made by distributed NoSQL stores.
Blockchains combine cryptographic hash pointers, digital signatures, and asymmetric key pairs.
Peer-to-peer gossip protocols form the networking foundation of decentralized blockchains.
Microcontroller programming requires understanding CPU registers, buses, and hardware memory maps.
Embedded firmware is almost universally authored in C due to precise hardware memory control.
Knowledge graph triples and OWL ontologies are grounded in discrete relations and first-order logic.
Graph query languages (SPARQL/Cypher) extend declarative query optimization principles.
Modern ASR systems rely on deep recurrent, transformer, and convolutional neural architectures.
Multimodal models extend deep representation learning across vision and text transformers.
Vision feature extraction provides foundational representations for vision-language models.
Tokenization and text transformer architectures are core components of multimodal foundation models.
Discrete optimization builds on linear programming duality, convex relaxations, and simplex algorithms.
Bayesian inference directly applies conditional probability, likelihood functions, and prior distributions.
Deep RL requires foundational understanding of Bellman equations and value iterations.
Deep neural networks serve as the function approximators for high-dimensional policies and Q-functions.
Edge AI focuses on compressing and accelerating deep neural networks for microcontroller deployment.
Embedded systems hardware understanding enables tuning ML models to real-time microcontroller constraints.
Entropy and mutual information are fundamental expectations over discrete probability distributions.
Formal game formulations use discrete strategy sets, bipartite matchings, and combinatorial trees.
Vector index algorithms like HNSW and IVF-PQ rely heavily on graph and partition data structures.
Vector search depends on inner products, cosine similarity, and high-dimensional vector spaces.
Technical communication and documentation principles enhance software requirement specifications and team reviews.
Shell scripting, server management, and Linux process controls are essential practical skills for CI/CD engineering.
Human-computer interaction and usability heuristics guide user-friendly frontend interface design.
